title: Afghan conflict
description: Near-continuous series of wars in Afghanistan
wiki_lead:
The Afghan conflict (Pashto: دافغانستان جنګونه; Farsi/Dari: درگیری افغانستان) is the series of events that have kept Afghanistan in a near-continuous state of armed conflict since the 1970s. Early instability followed the collapse of the Kingdom of Afghanistan in the largely non-violent 1973 coup d'état, which deposed Afghan monarch Mohammad Zahir Shah in absentia, ending his 40-year-long reign. With the concurrent establishment of the Republic of Afghanistan, headed by Mohammad Daoud Khan, the country's relatively peaceful and stable period in modern history came to an end. However, all-out fighting did not erupt until after 1978, when the Saur Revolution violently overthrew Khan's government and established the Democratic Republic of Afghanistan. Subsequent unrest over the radical reforms that were being pushed by the then-ruling People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan (PDPA) led to unprecedented violence, prompting a large-scale pro-PDPA military intervention by the Soviet Union in 1979. In the ensuing Soviet–Afghan War, the anti-Soviet Afghan mujahideen received extensive support from Pakistan, the United States, and Saudi Arabia in a joint covert effort that was dubbed Operation Cyclone.
Although the Soviets withdrew from Afghanistan in 1989, the various mujahideen factions continued to fight against the PDPA government, which collapsed in the face of the Peshawar Accord in 1992. However, the Peshawar Accord failed to remain intact in light of the mujahideen's representatives' inability to reach an agreement on a power-sharing coalition for the new government, triggering a multi-sided civil war between them. By 1996, the Taliban, supported by Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence, had seized the capital city of Kabul in addition to approximately 90% of the country, while northern Afghanistan remained under the authority of the anti-Taliban Northern Alliance. During this time, the Northern Alliance's Islamic State of Afghanistan enjoyed widespread international recognition and was represented at the United Nations, as opposed to the Taliban's Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan which only received diplomatic recognition from three nations. Despite the fall of Kabul to the Taliban, the Northern Alliance continued to resist in another civil war for the next five years.
After the September 11 attacks against the United States, which were carried out by the Afghanistan-based group al-Qaeda, the Taliban refused demands by the Bush administration to extradite al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden. This prompted the American-led invasion of Taliban-controlled Afghanistan, which bolstered the Northern Alliance by toppling the Islamic Emirate and installing the Afghan Transitional Authority in 2002. The invasion triggered the 20-year-long War in Afghanistan, in which NATO and NATO-allied countries fought alongside the nascent Islamic Republic of Afghanistan to combat the Taliban insurgency. During the Battle of Tora Bora, the American-led military coalition failed to capture bin Laden, who subsequently relocated to Pakistan and remained there until he was killed by U.S. SEAL Team Six in Abbottabad in 2011. Nonetheless, the fighting in Afghanistan continued, eventually leading to the 2020–2021 American withdrawal and ultimately ending with the 2021 Taliban offensive, which led to the re-establishment of the present-day Islamic Emirate.
Though the country-wide war ended in 2021, clashes and unrest currently persist in some parts of Afghanistan due to the ISIS–Taliban conflict and the anti-Taliban Republican insurgency. Additional cross-border fighting between Afghanistan and Pakistan has taken place since 2021, due to the former's continued support for the Pakistani Taliban. As of 2026, the collapsed Islamic Republic of Afghanistan remains the internationally recognized government of the country.

grok_lead: The Afghan conflict encompasses a chain of interconnected wars and insurgencies in Afghanistan spanning from the 1978 Saur Revolution through the present day, involving domestic power struggles, foreign military interventions by the Soviet Union and a US-led coalition, and the rise and persistence of Islamist factions such as the Taliban, resulting in over two million deaths and the displacement of millions more. The conflict's initial phase began with the Soviet-backed communist coup in April 1978, which provoked widespread rural uprisings against the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan regime's radical land reforms and secular policies; the Soviet Union invaded in December 1979 to stabilize its client government, deploying up to 120,000 troops that faced guerrilla warfare from mujahideen fighters supported by US, Pakistani, Saudi, and Chinese aid. This Soviet-Afghan War (1979â1989) inflicted approximately 13,800 Soviet deaths and over 1.3 million Afghan fatalities, including combatants and civilians, while failing to subdue the resistance and accelerating the Soviet Union 's internal collapse, leading to a full withdrawal by February 1989 under the Geneva Accords. The ensuing power vacuum triggered a civil war (1989â1996) among mujahideen factions, exacerbated by ethnic divisions and warlordism, which the Talibanâa Pashtun-dominated Islamist movement originating from Pakistani madrassasâexploited to seize Kabul in 1996 and control most of the country by 2001, imposing strict sharia governance amid ongoing factional fighting. The Taliban's harboring of al-Qaeda, responsible for the September 11, 2001, attacks on the United States, prompted a US-led invasion on October 7, 2001, under Operation Enduring Freedom, which rapidly ousted the Taliban regime through airpower and alliances with Northern Alliance forces but transitioned into a protracted counterinsurgency against Taliban resurgence, involving NATO troops and costing over 2,400 US military lives alongside tens of thousands of Afghan security forces and civilian casualties. Efforts to build a centralized Afghan state under Presidents Hamid Karzai and Ashraf Ghani faltered due to corruption, ineffective governance, and insufficient local legitimacy, enabling the Taliban âbolstered by cross-border sanctuariesâto regain momentum; the 2020 Doha Agreement between the US and Taliban set a withdrawal timeline, culminating in the Afghan National Defense and Security Forces' collapse and the Taliban 's unopposed capture of Kabul on August 15, 2021, restoring their rule and triggering a humanitarian crisis marked by economic isolation and restrictions on women. This sequence underscores recurring patterns of external powers underestimating Afghanistan's decentralized tribal structures and the enduring appeal of Islamist ideologies amid weak state institutions.
